name: Pinochetism
summary: Pinochetism is the doctrine of the Chilean military regime of Augusto Pinochet (1973-1990): a free-market economy designed by the Chicago Boys and a subsidiary state, joined to strong centralized authority, militant anticommunism and a guardian role for the armed forces. It holds that the 1973 coup saved Chile from Marxist totalitarianism and that a 'protected' democracy, with limited pluralism and the Marxist left excluded, must replace the pre-1973 party system. Its social outlook is nationalist, Catholic-conservative and family-centered.

notes: Answers rest on the 1980 Constitution (s7, original text), Pinochet's 1983 Mensaje Presidencial (s5) and Huneeus (s1); the IACHR report (s6) is cited for the Art. 8 and emergency provisions. Themes searched: economy, property, labour and unions, central bank and fiscal limits, education and health provision, government structure and the armed forces, party and speech limits, emergency powers, family, religion, citizenship and franchise, regionalization. Themes with no recorded position (world order, ecology, technology, gender identity, most moral and cultural issues) stay null. A 0 appears only where one text pulls both ways.
scope: The ideology of the Chilean military regime of 1973-1990 and of its civilian supporters, named after Augusto Pinochet: anticommunism, authoritarianism, militarism, conservatism, patriotism, nationalism and neoliberalism (Radio Universidad de Chile, 2018), joined to a guardian role for the armed forces under the 1980 Constitution and a 'protected democracy' (IACHR 1985). Huneeus records the gremialistas declaring themselves 'pinochetistas' in 1978, so the label covers the civilian right that backed Pinochet personally. The post-1990 'pinochetista' stance of today's Chilean right counts only as the sources describe it as the same current.
